Here are the strategies you can use to adapt your teaching: Include a statement about the use of these tools in your syllabi and assignments. Consider alternative ways to assess students' learning that require them to complete tasks outside of or in addition to tasks in ICON, such as oral presentations, visual or multimodal projects, case studies, and journals. units.passage: The increased “intellisense” functionality of tools like GitHub Copilot can enable AI to generate the “routine” or boilerplate code blocks for basic functions more quickly as it predicts what you need to accomplish in code.
units.why: Tools like GitHub Copilot 'can enable AI to generate the routine or boilerplate code blocks', which permits AI built into development tools (P07).
units.fit_note: Coder A: Permits IDE-integrated generation of routine code; it does not tell students to disable it. Coder B: Describes IDE assistants positively; no rule about disabling.

units.passage: Even if you choose to implement a Generative AI ban, explaining how Generative AI could, but shouldn’t, be used, and why, on specific assignments will help students navigate a digital environment in which Generative AI is increasingly integrated into search tools, e-books, Microsoft and Google products, etc.
units.why: Notes AI is 'increasingly integrated into search tools, e-books, Microsoft and Google products'; a fact about embedded AI that bears on bans, so P07 is the nearest type, as information only.
units.fit_note: States the fact of embedded AI as the reason to explain rules; does not itself cover or require disabling it. | Only notes that AI is embedded in common tools; it states no rule about them here.

units.passage: If using an e-book or search engine that has integrated Generative AI, then you should not rely on the Generative AI output and engage instead with the source material.
units.why: Covers search engines and e-books with integrated AI: do 'not rely on the Generative AI output'; embedded AI (P07), with a should-not.
units.fit_note: Allows the tool but tells students to engage with source material rather than rely on the AI output.

units.passage: you are not allowed to use AI for your coursework beyond these limited non-substantive supports
units.why: The same tier accepts AI embedded in everyday tools such as Word grammar check but says 'you are not allowed to use AI for your coursework beyond these limited non-substantive supports'. This covers embedded AI, so P07.
units.fit_note: Allows only non-substantive embedded features (grammar check, design suggestions, search) even in the no-AI tier. | Carves out limited non-substantive AI built into Word, PowerPoint and search engines while banning other AI use.

units.passage: Consider that AI is ubiquitous and embedded in many writing tools (for example, Grammarly, online translators, and Googe Docs autocomplete). AI tools are also widely used to generate visual and audio content.
units.why: 'AI is ubiquitous and embedded in many writing tools (for example, Grammarly, online translators, and Googe Docs autocomplete)' names embedded AI as part of the context: P07, informing.

units.passage: Smart in-context code completion such as GitHub Copilot (free for students).
units.why: Listing "Smart in-context code completion such as GitHub Copilot" as "Acceptable/encouraged" permits AI built into the editor: P07 fits better than P16 because the rule is about completion tools.
units.fit_note: Permits and encourages editor code completion (the opposite of requiring students to disable it); that the tool is free for students is also noted. / Also covers editor-integrated completion and a duty to verify the generated code.

units.passage: Large language model-powered code completion tools: GitHub Copilot, JetBrains AI Assistant…
units.why: The scope list names "Large language model-powered code completion tools: GitHub Copilot, JetBrains AI Assistant" and OS "AI features in Microsoft Windows", extending the policy to editor and OS AI: P07.
units.fit_note: A scope definition naming code completion and OS assistants; no instruction to disable them is stated here.

units.passage: Tools like GitHub Copilot that auto-complete code, suggest functions, or generate entire code snippets based on comments and context.
units.policy: GitHub Copilot, which auto-completes code, suggests functions, or generates entire code snippets, is an example of generative AI.
units.why: Listing GitHub Copilot among generative AI tools that 'auto-complete code' brings code assistants into the definition by example only, so P07 with a fit note.
units.fit_note: Names a coding assistant as an example of generative AI; sets no rule for editors or IDEs.

units.passage: Also, be aware that GenAI tools comprise stand-alone tools, such as ChatGPT, and GenAI functionality, which is increasingly embedded in a range of technologies. In these situations, it may not always be apparent to students when or if they are using GenAI tools. This is an important consideration in terms of punitive consequences.
units.policy: GenAI functionality is increasingly embedded in a range of technologies, so it may not always be apparent to students when or if they are using GenAI tools.
units.why: The note says GenAI is 'increasingly embedded in a range of technologies' so students may not know when they use it. That addresses AI built into other tools (P07), as a consideration rather than a rule.
units.fit_note: Informs instructors of embedded AI rather than regulating it.

units.passage: Faculty should try to remain aware of these features and help students understand when AI is involved.
units.why: "Faculty should try to remain aware of these features and help students understand when AI is involved." Covers AI built into word processors and LMS, so P07.
units.fit_note: Asks for awareness and explanation to students; it does not require disabling features.

units.passage: Students should not assume that a tool does not use AI simply because it is familiar.
units.why: "Students should not assume that a tool does not use AI simply because it is familiar" covers AI built into everyday tools, P07.
units.fit_note: Asks for awareness; it does not require disabling features. | Asks students to recognize embedded AI; does not say to disable it.

units.passage: Examples of these tools include ChatGPT, Claude, and NotebookLM, but also tools integrated into other platforms, such as Grammarly, and chat bots in research databases.
units.why: Says AI is also "integrated into other platforms, such as Grammarly, and chat bots in research databases", so the scope covers AI embedded in other tools (P07, nearest).
units.fit_note: Concerns AI embedded in writing and research platforms rather than editors, IDEs or agents; no rule is attached.

units.passage: Given the integration of generative AI tools into commonly used tools, students should receive written guidance from faculty on which applications of generative AI are not permitted.
units.why: Because AI is built into common tools, "students should receive written guidance from faculty on which applications of generative AI are not permitted". The duty falls on faculty to state in writing which embedded applications are not allowed (P07, course-start, should); it sets no ban of its own.
units.fit_note: Does not require disabling embedded AI; asks faculty to state in writing which applications are not permitted.

units.passage: If a professor has not permitted the use of AI tools, then using the generative AI function in Grammarly or CoPilot to create part of a draft may violate the Honor Code.
units.why: "If a professor has not permitted the use of AI tools, then using the generative AI function in Grammarly or CoPilot to create part of a draft may violate the Honor Code" tells students not to use built-in generative functions when AI is not permitted; the hedge "may violate" makes it should-not, and the tools are embedded ones, so P07.
units.fit_note: Conditional on the professor not permitting AI; it names Grammarly and Copilot as embedded tools. Also states a default that unpermitted generative drafting may violate the Honor Code.

units.passage: If you plan to use Grammarly and your professor has banned the use of AI tools, please make sure you have turned the generative AI function off
units.policy: If a professor has banned the use of AI tools, students who use Grammarly must turn the generative AI function off.
units.why: Students who use Grammarly where AI is banned must have "turned the generative AI function off". That is a requirement to disable an embedded AI feature, which P07 names.

units.passage: While it’s a student-directed tool (not predictive or automatic), it still carries the same academic integrity risks as ChatGPT or Copilot if used improperly.
units.why: Generative AI in Grammarly "still carries the same academic integrity risks as ChatGPT or Copilot if used improperly", extending the integrity warning to an embedded tool; informs, general, P07 (built-in tool) rather than P36 because it warns of risk and does not classify conduct as misconduct.
units.fit_note: A risk warning, not a classification of conduct as misconduct.

units.passage: An engineering student uses an advanced coding agent, such as ChatGPT Codex, to generate software for a complex project via natural-language prompting
units.why: An engineer 'uses an advanced coding agent, such as ChatGPT Codex, to generate software for a complex project', so coding agents are allowed at Level 4: P07.
units.fit_note: Describes a permitted use of an autonomous coding agent; the type is mainly about rules for embedded tools and agents. Covers allowing an autonomous coding agent at Level 4 rather than restricting it.

units.passage: AI-powered bots and agents can be valuable for automating workflows and providing quick assistance. Popular examples include OpenClaw (previously known as ClawdBot and MoltBot), Hermes Agent, and the many variants they have inspired, such as IronClaw, NanoClaw, and ZeroClaw. However, bots that are poorly scoped or improperly configured can introduce real risks: data exposure, unintended actions, or outputs that carry institutional weight without appropriate review. As the person deploying an AI agent, you are accountable for its actions. Approach deployment thoughtfully, ensure agents are properly sandboxed and clearly scoped in what data they can access and what actions they can take, and seek guidance before going live. The guiding principles in this document apply fully to AI agents.
units.why: 'As the person deploying an AI agent, you are accountable for its actions' sets responsibility for autonomous agents: P07 (covers agents), must.
units.fit_note: Rule on accountability for deploying agents, not on coding or editor use. Covers agents generally, not editors or IDEs.

units.passage: This includes chatbots like ChatGPT and Copilot, image generators, coding assistants, and similar technologies.
units.why: The prohibition template lists 'chatbots like ChatGPT and Copilot, image generators, coding assistants', covering built-in assistants: P07 fits partly.
units.fit_note: Lists coding assistants and chatbots as covered by the ban but does not mention editor integration. Lists tool categories covered; does not mention disabling editor features.

units.passage: You may not receive help from any AI tools including editing applications (e.g., Grammarly), generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT), or AI tools integrated within software platforms (e.g., Microsoft Office)
units.why: 'or AI tools integrated within software platforms (e.g., Microsoft Office)' extends the Category 1 ban to AI built into software, P07.
